In the last days, people will be lovers of self. All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable. Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season. The time of departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.

Come before winter. Bring the cloak, the books, and above all the parchments. Demas has gone to Thessalonica, loving the present world. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark; he is useful. Alexander the coppersmith did much harm. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. Grace. What is left open is whether Timothy will come in time, and whether the deposit will be guarded after Paul is gone.

2 Timothy is apostolic loneliness without self-pity. Hard parts include the deserted man, the harsh names, and a view of last days that later readers have always thought were theirs. Famous verses need their setting: God-breathed Scripture is profitable for a minister under pressure, not a theory floating free; I have fought the good fight is a last accounting, not a chant for winners; come before winter is a cloak and a friend, not a metaphor. The gospel is not chained. The apostle is.
titus: Titus is left in Crete to appoint elders and to put what remains in order. It is a short pastoral letter, written so that sound doctrine will produce sound lives: a whole community whose conduct does not give opponents an easy shot. The Protestant canon keeps it with 1 and 2 Timothy. It belongs because a church on a rough island needed a start, not a treatise, and because grace in this letter trains as well as saves.

Paul, a servant, to Titus, a true child in a common faith. Elders must be above reproach, not arrogant, not greedy, holding firm to the trustworthy word. Cretans are quoted against themselves; rebuke them sharply. The opening is a job description and a hard island.

Older men, older women, younger women, younger men, slaves — a whole household of instruction. Grace has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. He saved us not because of works done in righteousness, but according to his mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.

Be submissive to rulers. Avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions. Insist on good works. Help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way. What is left open is Crete itself: whether elders will be appointed, and whether a people with a bad reputation will become a people of good works. The letter is short because Crete needed a start, not a treatise.

Read grace as training, not as a mood. Hard parts include the Cretan proverb, slave instruction, and a tightness about order that later churches have over-loved. Famous verses need their setting: he saved us according to his mercy sits next to insist on good works; the blessed hope is an appearing, not an escape hatch from ordinary life. Sound doctrine here is a way of life that does not make the word ugly on an island that already has a proverb about lying.
philemon: Philemon is a private letter that became Scripture. Onesimus, an enslaved man, has left Philemon’s house, met Paul in prison, and become a Christian. Paul sends him back, not as a slave but as a beloved brother, and offers to pay whatever is owed. The Protestant canon keeps this scrap because the gospel had to land in a household, not only in a congregation. It is not a manifesto that pretends Rome was not built on slavery. It is a man putting his own credit on the line for someone with no status.

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, to Philemon our beloved fellow worker, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the church in Philemon’s house. Thanksgiving for Philemon’s love and faith. The opening is courtesy with weight. This is a man Paul loves.

The ask is large. Roman households ran on slavery. Paul does not write a manifesto. He writes a partner and puts their partnership in the scales. Onesimus, once useless, now useful — a pun on the name — has become Paul’s child in chains. Receive him as you would receive me. If he owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. Refresh my heart in Christ. A guest room is requested, as if Paul might come and see what was done.

Grace. What is left open is Philemon’s yes — and whether Onesimus will be received as a brother in the flesh and in the Lord. Colossians, sent by the same hands, names Onesimus a faithful and beloved brother. The letter does not narrate the outcome. The church kept the ask.

Read it as a household letter, not as a tract that solves the empire. Hard parts are the sending back, the missing legal manumission, and the courtesy that can sound like pressure because it is pressure. Famous lines need their setting: no longer a slave but a beloved brother is the gospel in a house that still has a door and a ledger. Receive him as you would receive me is Paul’s own body put in the place of a man with no status.
hebrews: Hebrews is a sermon in a letter’s clothes. Long ago God spoke by the prophets; in these last days he has spoken by a Son. It is written for believers, almost certainly with a Jewish Christian past, who are tired and might go back to something safer. The Protestant canon keeps it among the letters, though it names no author in the text. It belongs because it reads the tent, the priesthood, and the sacrifices of Israel as a copy now fulfilled, and because it will not let a weary church drift.

It begins with a cascade: the Son is heir, radiance, exact imprint, upholder of all things, seated after making purification, better than angels. A warning follows at once: do not neglect so great a salvation. The opening is worship and alarm together. This is not a polite preface. It is a claim that the last word has been spoken, and that drifting from it is not a small thing.

The argument runs by comparison. Jesus is counted worthy of more glory than Moses. A sabbath rest remains; today, if you hear his voice. The word of God is living and active. A great high priest who sympathises, who in the days of his flesh offered up prayers with loud cries. Melchizedek. A better covenant. The earthly sanctuary a copy; without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness; he offered himself once for all. Draw near. Do not throw away confidence. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for — and then a roll-call: Abel, Abraham, Moses, Rahab, a people of whom the world was not worthy.

Jesus is the pioneer and perfecter of faith. Discipline is treated as sonship. The mountain is Zion, not Sinai. Let us go to him outside the camp. Brotherly love, marriage, money; a sacrifice of praise. The God of peace brought up from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd. What is left open is the race still to be run, and a city that is to come. Hebrews does not end with a travel plan. It ends with a people looking for a city.

Read it as a sermon that expects to be heard in one sitting, even if that is hard. The hard parts are famous: the impossibility of restoring to repentance those who fall away; the living word that divides; a consuming fire. Famous verses need their setting: faith is the assurance sits at the head of a catalogue of people who died without receiving the promise; Jesus the same yesterday, today, and forever is a warning against strange teachings, not a motto for inertia. Leviticus is the other half of this book. Hebrews is for tired believers who might go back to something safer. Draw near is the invitation. Outside the camp is the cost.
james: James is a letter of practice. It is written to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion — scattered believers — in the name of James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. The Protestant canon keeps it among the catholic letters, after Hebrews. It belongs because the church needed a voice that would not let ‘faith’ mean agreement without a life. James is not a rival to Paul. It is a refusal to let hearing replace doing.

Count it joy when you meet trials. Ask for wisdom. The lowly brother is exalted; the rich fade. Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Religion that is pure and undefiled visits orphans and widows in their affliction and keeps oneself unstained from the world. The opening is almost a sheet of proverbs, then a stab: partiality toward the rich in assembly is sin.

Faith without works is dead. Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and Rahab when she received the messengers — a faith completed by what they did. The tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity. Wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits. Quarrels come from passions. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. Draw near to God. Do not speak evil of one another. If the Lord wills, we will live.

The rich are warned; unpaid wages cry out. Be patient until the coming of the Lord. The Judge is at the door. Elijah prayed. If anyone among you wanders from the truth, bring him back. What is left open is the wanderer, and whether the assembly will be a place of mercy or of gold rings at the front.

James is not a rival to Paul. Galatians fights a supplemented Christ; James fights a faith that will not feed a brother. Hard parts include the tongue, the rich, and the word justified, which must be read as a different question, not as a contradiction to Romans. Famous verses need their setting: faith without works is dead sits next to a brother or sister lacking daily food; count it all joy is trials, not a mood; the prayer of faith for the sick is a community act with oil and confession. If you say you believe and your brother or sister lacks daily food, what good is that?
1peter: 1 Peter is written to elect exiles of the dispersion — scattered believers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, under pressure. It is a letter of living hope, holiness, and a suffering that is not a surprise. The Protestant canon keeps it among the catholic letters. It belongs because the church needed a word for people who were resident aliens in their own towns, and because it names them a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, without pretending the fiery trial is light.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Born again to a living hope through the resurrection. An inheritance imperishable, undefiled, unfading. For a little while they suffer, so that the tested genuineness of their faith may result in praise. The opening is blessing, not a list of rules. Hope is the first gift.

Be holy, for he is holy. Love one another earnestly from a pure heart. Like living stones they are built into a spiritual house. Submit to the emperor; servants, follow Christ who suffered, leaving an example. Wives, husbands; honour everyone. Always be prepared to make a defence with gentleness and respect. Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God. Baptism now saves — an appeal to God for a good conscience — through the resurrection. Arm yourselves. Love covers a multitude of sins. Do not be surprised at the fiery trial.

Shepherd the flock, not under compulsion. Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God. Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you. Resist the devil. The God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. Peace. What is left open is the little while, and the glory after it.

Read it as a letter to exiles, not as a general essay on suffering. Hard parts include the household code, the emperor, and a devil who prowls. Famous verses need their setting: a royal priesthood is a people who were not a people, not a career in religion; cast all your anxieties sits next to humility and a roaring lion; always be prepared to make a defence is gentleness under slander, not a hobby of argument. Christ suffered for you, leaving an example. The example is not decorative.
2peter: 2 Peter is a farewell and a warning. It is a letter in Peter’s name to those who have obtained a faith of equal standing, written as if a tent were about to be folded. The Protestant canon keeps it despite its difficulty and its late welcome in some churches. It belongs as a last charge to grow, and as a refusal to let delay empty the promise of his coming.

Supplement faith with virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection, love. Make the calling and election sure. We were eyewitnesses of his majesty on the holy mountain. The prophetic word is more fully confirmed, a lamp in a dark place. The opening is growth and memory, not a rumour.

False teachers will come, as false prophets did. They will deny the Master who bought them, exploit with false words, promise freedom and be slaves of corruption. A donkey spoke with a human voice to restrain Balaam. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous under punishment. Scoffers will say, where is the promise of his coming? All things continue as they were. The delay is patience, not slackness. He does not want any to perish, but all to come to repentance. A thousand years as a day.

We are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. Be diligent to be found at peace. Paul has written of these things; some twist the hard parts. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be the glory. What is left open is the waiting, and whether growth will outrun the scoffing.

Read it as a farewell, not as a quarry for last-days charts. Hard parts include the delay, the fire, and a style denser than 1 Peter. Famous verses need their setting: a thousand years as one day is patience toward sinners, not a key for a lock; new heavens and a new earth is the hope that makes holiness make sense. Scoffers are not only future. They are the voice that treats delay as absence.
1john: 1 John is written so that its readers may know they have eternal life. It is a letter — or a sermon sent as a letter — from a witness who speaks of what they have heard and seen and touched: the Word of life. A community has split. The Protestant canon keeps it first of the three Johannine letters. It belongs because the church needed tests that were not merely moods: Jesus Christ come in the flesh, and love that is not only talk. God is light. God is love.

That which was from the beginning. Fellowship with the Father and with his Son. God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. If we say we have fellowship and walk in darkness, we lie. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive. The opening is testimony and a refusal of two lies: that sin is nothing, and that sin is everything.

An advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. An old commandment and a new one. Do not love the world. Antichrists have gone out. See what love the Father has given: we shall be like him. Love in deed and in truth. Test the spirits: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God. Perfect love casts out fear. We love because he first loved us.

I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life. Keep yourselves from idols. What is left open is the split: those who went out, and those who remain under the tests of flesh and love. Little children is the last address. The letter does not name the opponents so much as refuse their Jesus and their lovelessness.

The test is Jesus in the flesh, and love that is not only talk. Hard parts include the antichrists, a sin unto death, and a dualism of children of God and children of the devil that later readers have used cruelly. Famous verses need their setting: God is love sits in a chapter about brothers and sisters, not as a definition that erases judgment; if we confess is for people tempted to claim they have no sin; perfect love casts out fear is fear of punishment, not every tremor. These things are written that you may know. The knowing is fellowship, not a private certificate.
2john: 2 John is a postcard to the elect lady and her children — a church, or a woman and her household, loved in truth. It is the New Testament at its shortest-but-one, kept in the Protestant canon because truth and love had to share a page, and because hospitality was how teachers spread. It belongs as a line drawn at the door.

The elder to the elect lady. Grace, mercy, and peace in truth and love. I rejoiced to find some of your children walking in the truth. Love one another. This is love: that we walk according to his commandments. The opening is affection with a spine. The commandment is not new.

Many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh. Such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Watch yourselves. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting, lest you share in his wicked works. Hospitality was how teachers spread. The letter is drawing a line at the threshold.

I have much to write to you, but I would rather not use paper and ink. I hope to come and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete. The children of your elect sister greet you. What is left open is the visit, and whether the door will hold. Truth and love in one page, with a sharp edge on the threshold.

Read it with 1 John, not as a free-standing rule about visitors. Hard parts are obvious: the closed door, the withheld greeting, a line later churches have used against the wrong people. Famous verses need their setting: love one another is walking in the commandments; the deceiver is named by a doctrine — Jesus Christ coming in the flesh — not by manners. Face to face is the elder’s preference. Paper is the emergency.
3john: 3 John is to Gaius, whom the elder loves in truth. It is a private note about hospitality, authority, and a man who wants to be first. The Protestant canon keeps it as a small window on how the early churches treated travelling workers — and how a man who wants control can shut a door the gospel wanted open.

The elder to the beloved Gaius. I pray you may prosper in all things and be in health, as it is well with your soul. Fellow workers have testified to his hospitality, walking in the truth. You do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God, for they have gone out for the name, taking nothing from the Gentiles. The opening is thanks for an open house.

Diotrephes loves to be first, does not acknowledge the apostle’s authority, talks wicked nonsense, refuses the brothers, and puts people out of the church. The elder will come and bring up what he is doing. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and by the truth itself. Two names, two ways of holding a church.

Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name. What is left open is the visit, Diotrephes’ hold, and whether Gaius will keep the door open. A whole politics of the gospel sits in a note shorter than a chapter of Kings.

Read it as a window, not as a personality test for every difficult member. Hard parts include a public naming and a conflict over who may speak. Famous lines need their setting: loves to be first is a pastoral diagnosis, not a cheap insult; send them on in a manner worthy of God is money, food, and courage, not a sentiment. Greet the friends, each by name, is how a scattered church stays a church. The truth here has a guest room.
jude: Jude meant to write about their common salvation, and instead found he had to contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints. It is a short letter in the name of Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. The Protestant canon keeps it last before the unveiling. It belongs because grace can be perverted into sensuality, and because the church needed a warning that was also a doxology.

Beloved, certain people have crept in unnoticed, ungodly people who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. Mercy, peace, and love were the greeting; contention is the job.

Israel in the wilderness, angels who left their proper dwelling, Sodom and Gomorrah; these people are in the same path. Cain, Balaam, Korah. Hidden reefs at love feasts, waterless clouds, wandering stars. The Lord is coming with myriads of his holy ones to execute judgment. Enoch is quoted.

But you, beloved: remember the predictions of the apostles. Build yourselves up in your most holy faith. Pray in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. Have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire. Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy — the doxology that still ends services. What is left open is the keeping, and the fire from which some may still be snatched.

Read it as an emergency sermon, not as a licence to hunt. Hard parts include the extra-biblical examples, the severity, and a grace that is being used as cover. Famous verses need their setting: contend for the faith is not a hobby of argument; keep yourselves in the love of God sits next to a God who is able to keep you from stumbling. The doxology is not a pretty ending tacked on. It is the only safe last word after reefs and wandering stars.
revelation: Revelation is an unveiling, not a puzzle book. It is the last book of the Protestant canon: a prophecy in letters and visions, given to John on Patmos for seven churches in Asia, and kept by the church because the story of Scripture cannot end with a prison or a rumour. It belongs because it shows who actually rules when beasts look like they do, and because its last word is not a beast. It is a city, and a welcome.

John is on Patmos. He sees one like a son of man among seven lampstands, and writes to seven churches — Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea — commendation, warning, a promise to the one who conquers. First love lost, tribulation, a white stone, Jezebel, a name that lives and is dead, an open door, lukewarm water. Then a door in heaven, a throne, holy, holy, holy, and a slain Lamb who is worthy to open a scroll. The book begins on an island and in a throne room at once.

Seals, trumpets, bowls; a woman and a dragon; two beasts; Babylon falling; a rider on a white horse; a last rebellion; a great white throne. The pictures are piled, not lined up like a railway timetable. Four horses, souls under the altar, a multitude no one could count, locusts, two witnesses, a beast from the sea and a beast from the earth, a number, a harvest, bowls of wrath, a harlot city, a marriage supper. The centre is the Lamb, not the beasts. War in heaven is won by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.

Then a new heaven and a new earth, a holy city coming down, no more death, no more curse, the tree of life, a river, a face. The Spirit and the bride say, come. Surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. What is left open is the coming itself — promised, not scheduled. The Bible’s last word is not a beast. It is a city, and a welcome.

Read it as an unveiling of Jesus Christ, which is how it names itself, not as a codebook for tomorrow’s paper. Hard parts are almost the whole: numbers, beasts, bowls, and a history of readers who have been sure they had the timetable. Famous verses need their setting: I stand at the door and knock is spoken to lukewarm Laodicea, not as a generic evangelistic card; a new heaven and a new earth come after judgment, not instead of it. Daniel and Ezekiel and the prophets of Babylon are the other half of this book. The pictures are piled. The Lamb is at the centre. Come, Lord Jesus is a prayer, not a puzzle’s last clue.
